title: How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
body: How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner Health systems and startups are using the latest AI technologies to support clinicians, streamline workflows and improve patient care. November 13, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients. Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications. Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care. Friday, Nov. 13, 5:00 a.m. PT 🔗 Dyania Health Uses AI to Turn Decades of Patient Records Into Better Care Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts . Dyania Health , a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would. The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision. Keeping Patient Data Inside the Hospital Walls Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall.  The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital. Processing records this way takes chart review off the desks of clinical teams and lets them spend that time with patients. But Synapsis AI still requires clinician input — it’s an assistive tool that surfaces evidence from medical records that a clinician must still confirm and act on. Dyania builds and trains its clinical models with NVIDIA NeMo open libraries, then uses NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize them to run faster and more efficiently on the hospital’s own GPU servers. Synapsis AI in the Real World Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI to support a study of more than 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients between 2005 and 2021. Synapsis AI reasoned across each patient’s record, including every echocardiogram added in the years after surgery, and used this information to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and reintervention risk at the three-, five- and ten-year mark after a patient undergoes an aortic valve replacement procedure. The AI platform completed chart review across the full cohort that would have taken clinicians years to complete by hand. “Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” said Dr. Lars Svensson , chief of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic. The same approach can be applied to any healthcare challenge where the answer sits inside the medical record, such as identifying patients eligible for clinical trials, closing care gaps in cardiology and oncology, and populating clinical registries. Learn more about Dyania Health . Illinois Man Sentenced to Prison for Stealing Social Security Benefits
body: Press Release Illinois Man Sentenced to Prison for Stealing Social Security Benefits Friday, November 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Florida Tampa, Florida – Jonathan Frank Barner (55, Illinois) has been sentenced by U.S. District Judge John Baldalamenti to 15 months in federal prison for theft of government money. As part of his sentence, the court also entered an order of forfeiture in the amount of $107,175, the proceeds of the offense. Barner pleaded guilty on May 18, 2026. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement. According to court documents, from approximately May 2013 through April 2023, Barner continually accessed his deceased grandmother’s bank account to steal Social Security retirement insurance benefits intended for her. Incorrectly believing the grandmother to still be alive, the Social Security Administration continued to make deposits of monthly benefits into her bank account. Rather than reporting her death to the Social Security Administration, Barner continued to withdraw and spend the money on his own expenses until the Social Security Administration stopped making payments and the account was exhausted in April 2023. In total, Barner stole more than $107,000 belonging to the United States. This case was investigated by the Social Security Administration Office of the Inspector General. It was prosecuted by Special Assistant United States Attorney Matthew Del Mastro. The forfeiture was handled by Assistant United States Attorney Suzanne Nebesky. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. Updated November 13, 2026 Topic Financial Fraud Component USAO - Florida, Middle

title: HVAC Supplier Johnson Controls Inc. and Two Subsidiaries Agree to Pay $5 Million to Settle Cybersecurity Fraud Allegations
body: Press Release HVAC Supplier Johnson Controls Inc. and Two Subsidiaries Agree to Pay $5 Million to Settle Cybersecurity Fraud Allegations Friday, November 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Johnson Controls, Inc., of Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and two subsidiaries, Johnson Controls Fire Protection LP and Johnson Controls Security Solutions LLC (collectively, “Johnson Controls”), have agreed to pay $5 million to resolve allegations that they violated the False Claims Act by failing to comply with cybersecurity requirements in their federal contracts and subcontracts for building products and services, including heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) services. “Federal contractors must follow required cybersecurity standards to safeguard sensitive government information,” said Acting Assistant Attorney General Jonathan Guynn of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “The Justice Department will continue working with its law enforcement partners to ensure that federal agencies and taxpayers get what they paid for and to hold accountable government contractors who violate cybersecurity requirements.” The settlement resolves allegations that from January 2018 to August 2025, Johnson Controls entered into contracts and subcontracts with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the Departments of Defense, Energy, and Justice that required Johnson Controls to implement security controls to protect government information. Johnson Controls allegedly failed to control access to protected information due to a lack of sufficient information regarding its information systems and a lack of sufficient control over those systems. In addition, for contracts that required Johnson Controls to comply with cybersecurity controls in National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP) 800-171, including Department of Defense contracts, Johnson Controls allegedly failed to maintain a System Security Plan that met the contractual requirements and failed to adequately document, fully develop, or fully implement a plan of action and milestones to correct deficiencies and reduce or eliminate vulnerabilities in its information systems. “Cybersecurity requirements are of the utmost importance to the government,” said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “My office will vigorously pursue contractors who fail to follow these requirements, particularly when those failures persist over several years, needlessly exposing our nation to malevolent attacks and exploitation by bad actors." “Cybersecurity requirements in federal contracts are not optional.  They are binding obligations that protect sensitive government information,” said Director James Ives of the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS).  “Contractors who fail to meet these obligations jeopardize the security and trust fundamental to doing business with the federal government. DCIS and our law enforcement partners will continue to investigate violations and pursue accountability for contractors who disregard their cybersecurity obligations.” “Defense contractors who misrepresent their cybersecurity credentials and fail to safeguard critical infrastructure pose a direct threat to our Department of the Navy installations and warfighters,” said acting Special Agent in Charge Brian Merkal, Naval Criminal Investigative Service (NCIS) Economic Crimes Field Office. “NCIS and our federal partners will relentlessly pursue any company or contractor who cuts corners on security mandates and leaves us vulnerable to adversarial threats.” “A secure digital infrastructure is just as critical to NASA's operations as the physical building products and services Johnson Controls provides,” said Kathryn Sheehey, Senior Official at the NASA Office of Inspector General. “By failing to control access to sensitive information, this contractor put America’s space program at risk. Today’s settlement underscores that circumventing federal cybersecurity requirements incurs steep financial penalties.” “Government contractors must be honest and vigilant in protecting the sensitive information entrusted to them,” said Special Agent in Charge Floyd Martinez of the General Services Administration (GSA) Office of Inspector General (OIG) Southeast and Caribbean Investigations Division. “GSA OIG and our law enforcement partners remain committed to holding contractors accountable when they put national security at risk for financial gain.” The settlement resolves two qui tam or whistleblower lawsuits filed under the False Claims Act, under which private citizens can sue on behalf of the government and share in any recovery.  The settlement provides for the whistleblower, Kelly Vance, who formerly worked for Johnson Controls, to receive $850,000 as his share of the settlement.  The qui tam cases are captioned United States ex rel. Kelly Vance v. Johnson Controls, Inc. , No. 1:24-cv-2500 (N.D. Ga.) and United States ex rel. David Thomas v. Johnson Controls Int’l PLC , No. 1:26-cv-448 (D.D.C.). This year the Administration launched the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division to enhance the Administration’s war on fraud, waste, and abuse in federal programs. When unscrupulous actors exploit these programs for their own financial gain, they defraud the government, harm the people these programs are designed to aid and protect, and undermine American businesses that play by the rules. The Civil Division’s FCA enforcement plays a critical role in combatting such fraudulent schemes, recovering billions of dollars for the American taxpayers, and holding wrongdoers accountable. FCA matters will continue to be on the forefront of the battle against fraud, and the Civil Division’s FCA work will support and advance the mission of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The resolution obtained in this matter was the result of a coordinated effort between the Department of Justice Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, the U.S. Attorney’s Offices for the Northern District of Georgia and the District of Columbia, Defense Criminal Investigative Service, NCIS, Air Force Office of Special Investigations, NASA OIG, Department of Energy OIG, the Department of Justice OIG, and GSA OIG. The matter was handled by Trial Attorney Jennifer Cook, Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Nugent for the Northern District of Georgia, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Sean Tepe for the District of Columbia. The claims resolved by the settlement are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability. Note: The settlement can be found here . Updated November 13, 2026 Component Civil Division Press Release Number: 26-1360

title: Grand jury has indicted multiple defendants for immigration violations
body: Press Release Grand jury has indicted multiple defendants for immigration violations Friday, November 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Georgia SAVANNAH, Georgia: Multiple defendants have been indicted by the November term of the federal Grand Jury in the Southern District of Georgia for Re-entry after Removal or Deportation, a charge applied to an illegal alien present in the United States after at least one prior removal. Margaret E. “Meg” Heap, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Georgia, announced the indictments. Those facing federal charges include: Ruben Canos-Bences , 47, a citizen of Mexico, illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Glynn County. Evelio Gomez-Mateo , a/k/a Alexander Gomez, 45, a citizen of Guatemala, illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Effingham County. Roger Hernandez-Perez , 32, a citizen of Mexico illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Effingham County. Hilario Jimenez-Jimenez , 27, a citizen of Guatemala illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Coffee County. Alexis Yahir Itehua-Salas , 24, a citizen of Mexico illegally in the U.S., apprehended in Richmond County. Reentry after Removal or Deportation charges carry statutory penalties of up to two years in prison, followed by referral to immigration authorities for deportation. If a defendant’s removal is subsequent to a felony or aggravated felony, statutory penalties can be significantly more severe. Criminal indictments contain only charges; defendants are considered innocent unless and until proven guilty. These cases are being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and local law enforcement agencies and are being prosecuted for the United States by Southern District of Georgia Assistant U.S. Attorneys Olivia C. Brame, Bradley R. Thompson, and Joshua Kyle Davis. Contact For any questions, please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Office at (912) 652-4422. Updated November 13, 2026 Topic Immigration Component USAO - Georgia, Southern Press Release Number: 121-26

title: Florida Woman Sentenced for Scamming Millions of Dollars by E-mail
body: Press Release Florida Woman Sentenced for Scamming Millions of Dollars by E-mail Friday, November 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Virginia ABINGDON, Va. – A Florida woman who conspired with others to execute a business email compromise scheme to steal millions of dollars from victims throughout the United States was sentenced yesterday to 36 months in federal prison. Zamar McPherson, 50, of Boynton Beach, Florida, pled guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit bank and wire fraud and two counts of wire fraud. For her role in the conspiracy, McPherson was sentenced to imprisonment for a term of three years followed by three years of supervised release. In addition, she was ordered to forfeit $154,474.85.  McPherson was further ordered to pay restitution to four victims totaling over $1.5 million jointly and severally with her coconspirators. Two of McPherson’s coconspirators, Garland Shelton, 57, of Wytheville, Virginia, and Olivia Oxley, 35, of Brooklyn, New York, were sentenced earlier this year for their roles in the scheme. McPherson conspired with Shelton, Oxley, and others to engage in a business email compromise scheme.  The victims in this case had planned to send legitimate wire payments to certain payees.  A member of the conspiracy created and utilized fictitious email accounts, however, and provided new account information for the wire payments to the victims.  The victims were then defrauded into sending large sums of money to bank accounts belonging to McPherson, Shelton, and Oxley.  McPherson, Shelton, and Oxley created and utilized personal and illegitimate business accounts at various financial institutions to facilitate these fraudulent wire transfer payments. First Assistant United States Attorney Robert N. Tracci, Acting Special Agent in Charge Kai Wah Chan of Homeland Security Investigations Washington Division, and Ian Kaufmann, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI’s Richmond Division made the announcement. The case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, St. Paul, Minnesota, and the Eden Prairie, Minnesota Police Department with valuable assistance provided by Virginia State Police; Middlesex County, New Jersey Prosecutor’s Office; and Palm Beach County, Florida Sheriff’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Corey Hall is prosecuting the case. Updated November 13, 2026 Topic Financial Fraud Component USAO - Virginia, Western

title: From AI ambition to business impact
body: From AI ambition to business impact Nov 12, 2026 | Rodrigo Kede Lima - President, Microsoft Frontier Company Most business leaders I meet no longer need to be convinced that AI works. They’ve seen the pilots, the demos and the copilots. The question I hear in boardrooms now is different: How do we move from AI that impresses to AI that changes how the business actually runs? That is the question Microsoft Frontier Company was built to answer, and to date, we have engaged on nearly 500 projects with over 200 customers across 28 countries. Customers including 3M, Alaska Airlines, BMW, Core42, KT, Land O’Lakes, London Stock Exchange Group, Mastercard, McKesson, Northern Trust, Novo Nordisk, Publicis Groupe, Saint-Gobain, Siemens and Unilever are seeing real value from working side by side with our Forward Deployed Engineering teams. More importantly, most customers where we have completed initial projects have returned for additional engagements, generating hundreds of follow-on projects. Customers don’t come back for engineers. They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning. The technology is ready. What slows AI down is everything around it. That means identifying where AI can deliver the greatest value, building in trust and governance, redesigning the operating models and helping people work in new ways. Technology and people have to move forward together. What this looks like in practice Unilever is collaborating with Microsoft engineers to bring AI into its factories. On the factory floor, intelligent technology helps teams boost efficiency and deliver superior products to customers. In Pondicherry factory — Unilever’s largest Home Care Liquids factory in South Asia and a 2026 World Economic Forum Lighthouse site — a digital twin built on NVIDIA Omniverse and hosted on Azure simulates a real factory environment with integrated live data. This helps anticipate issues before they occur, monitors performance in real time and guides operators through the fixes and recommendations. 3M is working with our engineers to help its Global Business Services team automate customer order management. The companies are building an AI agent-driven workflow to assist with credit checks, delinquency assessments and system updates, with human-in-the-loop controls and a custom monitoring dashboard for real-time visibility and approvals. The solution is expected to significantly reduce manual effort, improve speed and consistency and accelerate cash flow — freeing staff for higher-value work while enabling scalable, auditable operations. Publicis Groupe is co-building with our engineers to bring AI into the heart of how it works and delivers for clients. Microsoft engineers work side by side with Publicis teams to design and build agentic processes grounded in Microsoft IQ, so agents work with the business context, data and knowledge behind Publicis’ work. These processes use reinforcement learning, drawing on real-world outcomes and human feedback to keep improving how the agents perform over time. The approach combines very fast engineering with hands-on knowledge transfer, helping Publicis build lasting AI capability. The work builds on Publicis’ rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to all 114,000 of its employees. Northern Trust needed to accelerate onboarding to its Asset Servicing Front Office Solutions platform, a process that took about two and a half weeks per client. Our engineers worked alongside Northern Trust’s experts to build an AI-powered onboarding agent within the Excel and SharePoint tools analysts already use. The result: data preparation time fell 83%, from two and a half weeks to three days, with 96.5% first pass quality score in testing . Analysts remain in control while gaining more time for higher-value client service. KT , one of South Korea’s largest telecommunications providers, wanted to help network operators identify and respond to problems faster. Our engineers worked from KT’s offices to co-build AIO-Net, a continuously learning AI agent platform informed by KT’s operating procedures and veteran network experts. It now detects network issues in two to three minutes, down from more than ten, while keeping people in control of decisions and actions. Saint-Gobain , the 360-year-old construction materials company, is using AI to help reduce the carbon footprint of cement. Working alongside its researchers, Microsoft engineers used Microsoft Discovery to gather 62,000 patents and 44,000 research abstracts into a knowledge base in hours, work Saint-Gobain estimates would have taken researchers a year. In about six weeks, the team identified new hypotheses for cement additives that scientists are now testing in the lab. Across all of these customers, the pattern is the same: Begin with the value , not the technology. Redesign the process , not just the task. Build in fast cycles with the customer’s teams. Put security, governance and cost management in place from day one , so scaling doesn’t stall. This is how organizations move from isolated AI projects to sustainable transformation: by focusing on measurable outcomes, redesigning work and building the capabilities to keep improving over time. New research from IDC underscores why this approach matters. While 66% of organizations report substantial or transformative results from AI, only 48% are scaling or seeing consistent value across their organizations. At the same time, 71% expect AI spending to increase by at least 10% in the next year, putting even greater pressure on businesses to demonstrate measurable returns. The challenge is no longer simply adopting AI. It is reimagining how work gets done and turning that transformation into lasting business impact. We’re holding ourselves to the same standard If we’re asking customers to redesign how they work around AI, we have to do the same. Microsoft Frontier Company was deliberately designed to be flat and fast, with one front door for customers, and as a reference for what an AI-native organization can look like. We are learning, adjusting and moving fast, the same way we ask our customers to. The real measure of success The gap between AI that impresses and AI that delivers won’t close on its own. It closes workflow by workflow, with people who understand the business sitting next to people who can build. Our success will be measured by more than what we deliver. The real test is what our customers can do after we’ve worked together: run, govern and improve their own AI systems, on their terms, with their intelligence protected. Their success is the clearest measure of ours. Learn more at www.microsoft.com/en-us/frontier-company . Rodrigo Kede Lima is the President of Microsoft Frontier Company and leads the operating business of 6,000 industry and engineering experts focused on delivering Frontier Transformation through AI for customers around the world. NOTE IDC Infographic, sponsored by Microsoft, The Real Business Value of AI, IDC #US54985026-IG, November 2026 Tags: AI , Azure , Microsoft 365 Copilot , Microsoft Frontier Company

Microsoft Frontier Company was deliberately designed to be flat and fast, with one front door for customers, and as a reference for what an AI-native organization can look like. We are learning, adjusting and moving fast, the same way we ask our customers to. The real measure of success The gap between AI that impresses and AI that delivers won’t close on its own. It closes workflow by workflow, with people who understand the business sitting next to people who can build. Our success will be measured by more than what we deliver. The real test is what our customers can do after we’ve worked together: run, govern and improve their own AI systems, on their terms, with their intelligence protected. Their success is the clearest measure of ours. Learn more at www.microsoft.com/en-us/frontier-company . Rodrigo Kede Lima is the President of Microsoft Frontier Company and leads the operating business of 6,000 industry and engineering experts focused on delivering Frontier Transformation through AI for customers around the world. title: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms
body: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms Nov 12, 2026 | Alysa Taylor - Chief Marketing Officer, Commercial Cloud & AI Results are widespread. Value at scale is not, and that gap is what this year’s research from IDC , commissioned by Microsoft, set out to explain. In our fourth year commissioning IDC, more than 5,200 senior IT and business leaders across 28 industries shared what it takes to maximize value as AI scales. The clearest lessons come from Frontier Firms, the group last year’s research introduced: the top 10% of organizations on IDC’s AI maturity scale. What the research found Frontier Firms lead on return. They report an average 4x return on AI versus 2.7x for slow adopters (the bottom 30% on IDC’s scale), and 39% see returns of 5x or more versus 4% of slow adopters. Measurement is the next test . Only 61% of organizations are highly confident they can measure AI’s business value and ROI, versus 93% of Frontier Firms. Governance is in place, but confidence lags. 65% of organizations have an established process to govern agents, yet only 60% have high confidence in addressing AI security and governance risks. Workforce readiness is uneven. 67% say their workforce reports high trust in AI, yet only 20% have a comprehensive, organization-wide skilling strategy. “Organizations that scale AI value aren’t simply spending more. They manage AI investments, models, agents, governance and skills as one discipline, and that is what turns early results into value they can repeat across the business,” says Kathy Lange, Research Director, AI, Data and Automation Software, IDC. AI value now reaches well beyond cost savings Organizations now use AI in 6.5 business areas on average, led by IT infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service, with the fastest growth in industry-specific uses. Employee experience, revenue growth, customer experience, innovation and risk reduction now rank nearly even as the places AI strengthens the business. Cost is an important consideration, but it is evaluated alongside accuracy, security, compliance and scalability. Where scale stalls 66% of leaders say AI has delivered substantial or transformative results, but only 48% are scaling that value across multiple business units. Agents follow the same pattern: 36% of organizations are still piloting them. The widest gap is people: workforce confidence is running well ahead of the plans to support it. The organizations pulling ahead are closing these gaps by design. Inside the Frontier Firm IDC’s maturity scale weighs spending discipline, breadth of use, agent adoption, skills, confidence in managing AI risk and outcomes. On agents specifically, Frontier Firms report a 3.8x return versus 3.0x for slow adopters. These returns are leader-reported, and the research shows association rather than cause. What they do differently comes down to five behaviors: They invest ahead of plan . 90% of Frontier Firms exceeded their planned AI spend. They deploy AI broadly , across most of the business, not just a few teams. They put agents to work . 96% are rolling out agents at scale, and 53% orchestrate them across workflows. They govern so they can scale . 87% have a process to govern and oversee agents, versus 51% of slow adopters. They build skills everywhere . 80% have an organization-wide AI skilling strategy, versus 3% of slow adopters. At Bristol Myers Squibb , the RABIT agent “connects the dots across meetings, helping teams make better decisions while reducing administrative follow-up work,” says Lakshman Yerramalla, Director of Portfolio Governance and Delivery for Global Manufacturing Operations. Project managers who use it save up to an estimated 20% of their time. Four disciplines for scaling AI value The lesson from Frontier Firms is one I believe every leader can act on: scaling AI value means managing models, agents, governance and measurement as one accountable system. Value and control aren’t a trade-off. I see the same pattern with customers: the organizations scaling fastest treat AI as a change in how the business runs, not a technology rollout. “The skilling that a lot of companies miss is the business skilling,” says Eric Tabor, Chief Digital Officer, KOHLER . “We also focus on how to dissect processes and convert them into AI workflows.” Unlock model choice Trust and security, leading-edge technology and model performance tie as the top criteria for choosing an AI platform (44% each). Match the right model to each job, balancing cost with protection of intellectual property and data. Redesign workflows around agents Agents create the most value when work is redesigned around them. The bigger opportunity is what they free people to do more of: leaders point to creativity, innovation and business reinvention (41%), customer-facing work and relationships (39%) and analytical work and data interpretation (39%). Connect agents across processes, with human oversight where it matters. Govern decisions and actions Trust is building faster than confidence. Most leaders report high trust in their AI systems, yet fewer are highly confident addressing security and governance risks. As agents take on more of the work, trust has to be earned continuously, and governance has to reach beyond models to keep people in control of what agents decide and do. Conagra Brands made governance its starting point. “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information Officer, Conagra Brands. “We built a SteerCo to review risk factors, access and identity management.” Measure and optimize value Connect investment and performance data to business outcomes, compare how processes perform before and after AI and direct spending where it delivers the most value. With 71% of organizations expecting AI budgets to rise 10% or more in the next 12 months, this discipline will separate leaders from the rest. Underneath all four disciplines are people. None of it scales without an organization-wide plan to build AI skills. That’s where Frontier Firms are furthest ahead, and it’s where I’d urge every leader to start. Black & Veatch reached 98% adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot through deliberate change management, including early-adopter cohorts that surfaced real business use cases. “Our goal is to be a Frontier Firm. The intention is not to stop at pure adoption,” says Mike Adams, Chief Digital Technology Officer, Black & Veatch. Go deeper at Microsoft Ignite IDC Executive Analyst Shari Lava will lead three sessions at Microsoft Ignite on Nov. 18, including The AI ROI Divide: Why Some Organizations Scale and Others Stall. What this means for business The gap that matters now isn’t between companies that use AI and those that don’t. It’s between those getting results in pockets and those turning AI into repeatable value across the business. There are three key ways leaders can step into this kind of transformation. First, treat AI as business transformation, not a technology rollout. Frontier Firms connect AI to the outcomes that matter most, from growth to customer experience, and manage it as one accountable system. That is the heart of Frontier Transformation, and it’s the work we’re doing alongside our customers every day. Second, start with your own function. In marketing, we’re applying these same disciplines to our own work: redesigning workflows around agents, setting clear guardrails and measuring what AI actually delivers. Every function can become its own proof point for the rest of the business. Third, invest in people as much as in technology. Skills are the widest gap in this year’s research, and it’s the one I care about most. The organizations that pull ahead will be the ones where everyone, at every level, has the support to learn, experiment and grow with AI. The next phase of AI won’t be defined by who uses it. It will be defined by who can scale its value and stay in control. This research gives every leader a benchmark for where they stand today and a clear view of what to do next. title: A New Dawn in the Cloud: ‘Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV’ Is Coming to GeForce NOW
body: A New Dawn in the Cloud: ‘Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV’ Is Coming to GeForce NOW Plus, catch NVIDIA DLSS 5 updates for ‘War Thunder’ and ‘Where Winds Meet,’ and dive into ‘Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen,’ alongside 10 new games. November 12, 2026 by GeForce NOW Community 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Rally the ranks this GFN Thursday. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV is coming to GeForce NOW , allowing players to experience the battle for Kronus through cloud gaming. There’s more on the horizon, with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology coming to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet . Meanwhile, Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen brings new tales and encounters, alongside 10 games joining the GeForce NOW library this week. Kronus Calls for Reinforcements Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV , developed by KING Art Games and published by Deep Silver, is coming to GeForce NOW. Launching on Steam Thursday, Dec. 3, the real-time strategy game returns to the series’ roots with large-scale battles, base building and a renewed fight for planet Kronus. Command the Space Marines, Orks, Necrons or the Adeptus Mechanicus, which makes their series debut. Build a base, secure resources and customize squads to the conflict across more than 70 campaign missions, playable solo or in co-op mode. The Last Stand, Skirmish and multiplayer modes offer more ways to put tactics to the test. GeForce NOW will bring the action to supported PCs, Macs, handhelds and other devices, with game downloads and updates handled in the cloud. Save the storage space for everyday essentials and planning for the next offensive. Wishlist the game on Steam , and stay tuned to GFN Thursday to prepare for launch. DLSS 5 Keeps on Coming NVIDIA DLSS 5 continues to evolve, with Gaijin Entertainment’s War Thunder and Everstone Studio’s Where Winds Meet next to receive support for the technology with the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature. Arriving in mid-November, War Thunder ’s Eagle’s Shadow major update adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, dozens of new planes, ships and tanks, along with cluster bombs for planes and visual-effects enhancements increasing the realism and dynamism of battle. In Where Winds Meet , DLSS support arrives Monday, Nov. 23, enhancing the environments and characters of its wuxia open-world action role-playing game. Both titles will use the latest DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model, released in October, which doubles model performance compared with the previous version. Since its initial announcement in March, model performance has improved tenfold, bringing the technology to more gamers, including GeForce NOW Ultimate members streaming with GeForce RTX 5080 cloud rigs. Get a closer look at the DLSS updates and find more details . A New Tale for the Arisen Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is streaming on GeForce NOW, expanding the deep, explorable fantasy world of Dragon’s Dogma 2 with new tales and encounters. Travel to the long-abandoned region of Norgan, join the enigmatic Eir and uncover the secrets of the undying Fallen Dragon. Unearth forgotten relics to unlock powerful weapons and skills, take on Lost Rites’ 12 dungeon challenges and explore new hairstyles and tattoos for Arisen and Pawn customization. Delicious in Dungeon also arrives in the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with a special collaboration. GeForce NOW keeps all the new downloadable content available across supported devices — without a single download claiming local storage on a gamer’s hardware of choice. In addition, members can look for the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week: Worst Class Ever (New release on Steam , Nov. 9) Ashes of the Singularity II (New release on Steam , Nov. 10) Cyberpunk 2077 ( Xbox Play Anywhere, new release on Battle.net , Nov. 10) DreamWorks Shrek 2 Remastered (New release on Steam , Nov. 10) Warhammer Survivors (New release on Steam and Xbox , available on Game Pass, Nov. 10) Main Sequence (New release on Steam , Nov. 12) Deadly Days: Roadtrip ( Steam ) GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend ( Steam , Ultimate members) Graveyard Keeper ( Steam ) Tape to Tape ( Steam ) Also this week, Ultimate members can take a trip back to 2006 with GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend , a playable demo celebrating the iconic GPU’s 20th anniversary with DLSS 4.5 and path tracing in the cloud. Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles. Those ready to put the next game plan into action can grab a day pass to try Performance or Ultimate, with the cost applicable toward a first monthly membership. What’s on the gaming lineup this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below. title: Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator
body:
Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , the AWS SDKs , and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub . You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker. How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged. From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region. The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS. If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally. Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023 . The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/ , so it’s on the path. PKG=https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest
sudo dnf install -y $PKG/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm

aws-emulator -v On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image. I started the emulator with aws-emulator . It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 , so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file. aws-emulator In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials. export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297
export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config
export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true
export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR , so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000 . curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health

aws sts get-caller-identity Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it. $ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started
make_bucket: local-getting-started

$ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt

$ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/
upload: ./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt

$ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/ With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them. Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account. kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables
      are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table
      "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item
      {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it
      back with get-item.

$ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \
    --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \
    --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

$ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \
    --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}'

$ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}' To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual. Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java . For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust . You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions};
use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{
    AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType,
    ScalarAttributeType,
};

#[tokio::test]
async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() {
    let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default());
    let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest())
        .http_client(emulator.http_client())
        .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1"))
        .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider())
        .load()
        .await;
    let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config);

    ddb.create_table()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .attribute_definitions(
            AttributeDefinition::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S)
                .build().unwrap())
        .key_schema(
            KeySchemaElement::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash)
                .build().unwrap())
        .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest)
        .send().await.unwrap();

    ddb.put_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();

    let got = ddb.get_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();
    assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi");
} When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off. How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates. With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better. If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub. How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline , and AWS CodeCommit , so it stays current with AWS as those models change. One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. retained_feed_body:
Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , the AWS SDKs , and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub . You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker. How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged. From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region. The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS. If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally. Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023 . The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/ , so it’s on the path. PKG=https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest
sudo dnf install -y $PKG/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm

aws-emulator -v On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image. I started the emulator with aws-emulator . It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 , so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file. aws-emulator In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials. export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297
export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config
export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true
export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR , so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000 . curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health

aws sts get-caller-identity Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it. $ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started
make_bucket: local-getting-started

$ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt

$ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/
upload: ./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt

$ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/ With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them. Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account. kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables
      are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table
      "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item
      {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it
      back with get-item.

$ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \
    --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \
    --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

$ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \
    --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}'

$ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}' To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual. Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java . For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust . You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions};
use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{
    AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType,
    ScalarAttributeType,
};

#[tokio::test]
async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() {
    let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default());
    let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest())
        .http_client(emulator.http_client())
        .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1"))
        .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider())
        .load()
        .await;
    let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config);

    ddb.create_table()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .attribute_definitions(
            AttributeDefinition::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S)
                .build().unwrap())
        .key_schema(
            KeySchemaElement::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash)
                .build().unwrap())
        .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest)
        .send().await.unwrap();

    ddb.put_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();

    let got = ddb.get_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();
    assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi");
